title: Teachers, Students, and Sleep
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that sleep is an overlooked lever for student and teacher motivation. Drawing on Maria Konnikova's New Yorker series and Shawn Stevenson's Sleep Smarter, he lists ten facts, covering how alcohol and irregular schedules degrade sleep, how sleep supports memory and insight, and how screens and lack of daylight disrupt melatonin. He ties regular sleep to better mood and GPA and says these findings belong in every teacher's conversations with students, not only in health class. A mid-post aside argues that sleep is another reason not to judge teachers by test scores, since teachers cannot control it. He concludes that because sleep improves both outcomes and daily quality of life, teachers and students should treat it seriously, including by limiting working hours.
points: Regularity of bedtime matters more than catching up on sleep, and inconsistent sleep schedules are linked to worse mood and grades.
Sleep does active cognitive work, consolidating memory and helping people discover shortcuts in problems.
Screen light within an hour or more of bedtime delays melatonin and shifts the body clock, so screens should end earlier.
Teachers should talk to students about sleep out of care for their long-term flourishing, not to raise test scores.
quotes: Let’s take a different tack on motivation, one that’s almost universally ignored. If my students sleep better, I bet they’ll self-motivate better. And so will you.

The key to higher quality, REM-filled sleep is regularity. Regular exercise helps us sleep better, as does a regular meal time and a regular bed time. In fact, one study suggests that sleep variability (i.e., going to bed at inconsistent times) is one of the most important factors in how well people sleep. It’s better, then, to go to bed at the same time each night rather than going to bed early tonight to “catch up” from a late one last night.

The point is that, just because Sleep-Deprived John does better than his peers with inadequate amounts of sleep doesn’t mean he couldn’t be 14 percent faster and 20 percent more accurate otherwise. (Not to mention happier; see #4).

First of all, sleep is one more reason why it is insane to measure teachers based on a few high stakes tests. I have no control over how much my students sleep all year long — and yes, that’s the sleep that matters, not just the sleep on the night before the test. Sleep, then, is one more reason why we are better off ignoring “your worth as a teacher is akin to your students’ test scores” messages and focusing on long-term flourishing instead.

I’m going to speak with my students about sleep this year because I love them and want the best for them, and so this information is worth their hearing. Some students will shrug if off; others will have a seed planted that won’t germinate for years; and still others will begin putting better sleep into practice and experience the beginnings of a quality-of-life increasing, success-predicting habit. In short, when I talk to my students about sleep, it won’t be to help their test scores; it will be because I am a teacher.

9. So chill on the screens. This is probably the easiest thing my students (and I) can work on: screen time needs to end at least an hour before bed (although the Czeisler study above suggests that even earlier would be better). When I set the alarm on my phone before climbing into bed, I now kind of awkwardly try to not look at it. This is probably the beginning of some kind of photophobic complex.

Sleep makes us more likely to succeed and more likely to enjoy each day. When something does both of those things — improves our outcomes in the future and our quality of life today — we’re silly to ignore it.
